title: 01 - Before We Start: Detailed Video Scripts
subtitle: Script-driven draft video. Available from May 18, 2026.

chapters.title: 1. Where We're Going
chapters.target: 10-12 minutes, talking head plus course-map slides and one terminal/diff preview.
chapters.onScreenText: Goal -> Context -> Plan -> Execute -> Verify -> Review -> Handoff
chapters.screenDirection: Show a simple course roadmap. Then show a final example task summary with sections: Goal, Files changed, Checks run, Risks, Next step.
demoSteps: Open a sample final handoff note.
Point to the changed files list.
Point to a remaining risk or follow-up.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write one sentence: what do you want AI coding to improve in your workflow? Then write one thing you do not want to give up control over.
chapters.recap: The goal is not to make the agent independent. The goal is to make the work controlled, visible, and faster.
beats: Most developers do not fail with AI coding because the model is useless. They fail because they treat the model like a magic box. This course is about something more practical: building a workflow where an AI coding agent can help you move faster without taking control away from you.

By the end of this course, you should be able to take a real repo task, shape it, give it to an agent, review what happened, run verification, and hand off the result. You will not just learn commands. You will learn a working system.

setup, agent harness basics, fundamentals, steering, planning, feedback loops, AFK agents, and human-in-the-loop patterns. Emphasize that each day adds a control layer and works across terminal-based agents, CLI agents, IDE agents, hosted agent apps, and similar tools.
shape the task, inspect the repo, choose HITL or AFK, execute a small slice, verify, review, summarize, and continue.
This is not a prompt-hacking course. It is not a replacement for engineering judgment. It is not about generating the most code. It is about getting useful, reviewable, verified work.

chapters.title: 2. Navigating The Discord
chapters.target: 8-10 minutes, screen recording of Discord structure or a mock community layout.
chapters.onScreenText: Goal. Context. Tried. Output. Expected. Question.
chapters.screenDirection: Show a mock help post. Highlight each required part with callouts.
demoSteps: Start with a weak post: "Migration failed. Help?
Rewrite it with exact command, error, environment, and question.
Show how the improved version invites a useful answer.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Create a help-request template you can reuse during the course.
chapters.recap: Good community questions are not longer. They are easier to reproduce.
beats: 'It does not work.' The fastest way to get helped is to make the problem easy to understand.
Explain that learners will use Discord for debugging, feedback, office-hour prep, sharing prompts, and comparing workflows.
Walk through announcements, help, cohort chat, office hours, project sharing, and wins. Tell learners where to ask setup questions versus workflow questions.
goal, context, command or prompt used, exact output, what you expected, and the precise question.
Explain why huge pasted logs, screenshots without text, vague complaints, and missing repo context slow everyone down.

chapters.title: 3. Repo Setup
chapters.onScreenText: A working baseline beats a confident guess.
chapters.screenDirection: Terminal on left, setup notes on right.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Create SETUP_NOTES.md with the commands that worked on your machine and any failures you hit.
chapters.recap: Before you ask an agent to change code, make sure both of you know how to tell whether the repo still works.
beats: If the repo does not run locally, the agent is not coding. It is guessing.
dependencies installed, local commands understood, and at least one verification command passing or failing for a known reason.
source, tests, docs, scripts, migrations, config, package or lock files.
Run or describe the install command. Explain that learners should capture versions and errors.
Run lint, test, typecheck, or app start command. Explain each result.

chapters.title: 4. Database Migrations
chapters.target: 10-13 minutes, conceptual explanation plus local migration demo.
chapters.onScreenText: Schema change = code risk + data risk
chapters.screenDirection: Show migrations folder, a sample migration, and schema diff or DB inspection command.
demoSteps: Draft a migration prompt with safety constraints.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a migration safety checklist with current schema, desired change, rollback, and verification.
chapters.recap: The agent can help with migrations, but the human owns the data risk.
beats: A bad code change can often be reverted. A bad database migration may have already changed the data.
Explain schema evolution as ordered, repeatable changes to database structure or data.
Show timestamp/name, up/down or apply/rollback, schema changes, and seed/data migrations.
Demonstrate running migrations locally and checking the result.
inspect existing models and migrations, propose shape, call out compatibility risks, do not run production changes.

chapters.title: 5. Setting Up Your Agent Harness For The Course
chapters.onScreenText: First task: inspect. Second task: plan. Third task: edit.
chapters.screenDirection: Terminal or IDE agent session, then editor showing repo files.
demoSteps: Open your chosen agent harness in the repo.
Ask for repo summary with no edits.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Save your default first prompt for a new codebase.
chapters.recap: Start every agent relationship with orientation, not action.
beats: Your first agent harness task should not be 'build my feature.' It should be 'show me you understand the repo.'
The chosen harness should be authenticated or configured, launched in the right repo, and able to inspect files safely.
Show current working directory and explain why launching from the wrong folder poisons the session.
Inspect this repo and tell me how to run it. Do not edit files.
Explain how different harnesses ask for approval, or how the human can enforce approval manually when the tool has weaker permission controls.

chapters.title: 6. How To Take This Course
chapters.target: 8-12 minutes, talking head plus note-taking demo.
chapters.screenDirection: Show a Markdown course journal being filled out.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Choose your practice repo and create your first course journal entry.
chapters.recap: The notes you write during failures will become your best agent instructions later.
beats: Watching this course will not change your workflow. Practicing the loops will.
Watch, pause, run, review, write a note.
lesson, prompt used, result, mistake, new rule.
Recommend using the same repo so lessons compound.
Pause before running commands, before approving edits, after failing checks, and before accepting a summary.

chapters.title: 7. Office Hours
chapters.screenDirection: Show a messy question being rewritten into a clear office-hours prompt.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Prepare one office-hours question using context, evidence, and decision needed.
chapters.recap: The clearer your question, the more useful the answer.
beats: Office hours are most useful when you bring evidence, not just confusion.
Explain that office hours are for stuck points, workflow review, task shaping, and decision support.
Current goal, repo state, prompt used, command output, error, expected result, and specific ask.
Is this scoped well?", "What verification is missing?", "Should this be HITL or AFK?", "Where is the review gate?
What should I build?", "Why is everything broken?", or anything without evidence.

chapters.title: 8. Appendix: Cohort 003 -> Cohort 004 Changelog
chapters.onScreenText: Current workflow wins over old notes.
chapters.screenDirection: Show a sample changelog table with "old guidance," "new guidance," and "why changed.
demoSteps: Explain the reason for the change.
chapters.exercisePrompt: If you have prior notes, mark anything that may be outdated. If not, write one question you have about the course evolution.
chapters.recap: The course will keep improving. Your workflow should too.
beats: A changelog is not trivia. It tells you what the course learned from previous learners.
Explain that tools, workflows, and course emphasis changed between cohorts.
New lessons, renamed workflows, removed advice, updated commands, and improved exercises.
If old Discord posts conflict with the current lesson, prefer the current lesson unless an instructor says otherwise.
Ask them to mark old notes that need updating.

title: 02 - Getting To Know Your Agent Harness: Detailed Video Scripts
subtitle: Script-driven draft video. Available from May 18, 2026.

chapters.title: 1. Intro
chapters.target: 8-10 minutes, terminal intro plus simple slides.
chapters.onScreenText: Agent harness = repo context + tools + review loop
chapters.screenDirection: Open your chosen agent harness in a repo. Ask for repo organization with no edits.
demoSteps: Launch your chosen agent harness in a repo.
Ask: "Inspect this project and tell me how it is organized. Do not edit files.
Review the response as orientation, not truth.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Run or write your first repo-safe prompt. It should ask for inspection only and forbid edits.
chapters.recap: An agent harness becomes useful when you pair its speed with your review loop.
beats: An agent harness is not just a chatbot that knows programming. It is a repo-aware collaborator that can inspect files, run commands, make edits, and explain what changed.
Explain that the value comes from connecting language, local files, shell commands, and review.
Ask, inspect, approve, run, review, continue." Walk through each word and what the learner does.
Session management, terminal prompting, IDE integration, moving through history, bash commands, and permissions.
The agent can propose and execute, but you own the repo, the review, and the decision to ship.

chapters.title: 2. Managing Your Agent Session
chapters.onScreenText: Path. Goal. Scope. State. Next step.
chapters.screenDirection: Show a session start checklist in one pane and terminal in another.
demoSteps: Ask the agent to summarize repo context.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Create a session-start checklist with path, goal, scope, git state, and first safe prompt.
chapters.recap: A focused session gives the agent fewer chances to guess.
beats: An agent session is not just a conversation. It is the working memory for the task.
Confirm current directory, repo name, branch, and task. Explain that the wrong starting directory causes wrong assumptions.
goal, scope, files inspected, commands run, decisions, and open questions.
When the agent drifts, restate the task and current facts instead of restarting emotionally.
Use a new session for unrelated tasks, polluted context, wrong repo, or a major direction change.

chapters.title: 3. Prompting In The Terminal
chapters.screenDirection: Show a table with weak prompt, problem, stronger prompt.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Rewrite three prompts from your own work using goal, scope, constraints, and done condition.
chapters.recap: The agent can only optimize for success if you define success.
beats: A prompt is a task contract. If the contract is vague, the agent fills in the blanks.
Teach goal, scope, constraints, and done condition. Give a one-sentence example of each.
Rewrite "fix the login bug" into "reproduce the failing login test, identify the smallest cause, patch only auth files unless evidence requires otherwise, and run the targeted test.
Explain explore-only, plan-only, edit, review, debug, and verify prompts. Each mode produces a different kind of output.
Show how to paste or reference a command failure and ask the agent to reason from the evidence.

chapters.title: 4. Your Agent Harness And Your IDE
chapters.target: 10-12 minutes, split screen terminal and IDE.
chapters.screenDirection: Split terminal and IDE diff view. Use callouts on changed files and review notes.
demoSteps: Ask the agent where a behavior lives.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Review one agent change in your IDE and write one risk before accepting the summary.
chapters.recap: The IDE is not replaced by the agent. It becomes your control panel.
beats: The agent can move quickly, but your IDE is where you should slow down and inspect.
The agent searches, explains, edits, and runs commands. The IDE helps you navigate, compare diffs, inspect symbols, and review.
Ask the agent to identify relevant files, then open them yourself.
Show changed lines, surrounding code, tests, and possible side effects.
Keep the behavior change, but revert the unrelated style cleanup.

chapters.title: 5. Going Forwards And Backwards In Time
chapters.onScreenText: Checkpoint before risk. Inspect before continue.
chapters.screenDirection: Terminal with git status and IDE diff.
demoSteps: Show how to revert that one change intentionally.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write your checkpoint rule: when will you commit, stash, or stop for review?
chapters.recap: If you can inspect and recover, you can let agents move faster without losing control.
beats: Agent work can move faster than your memory. Time travel keeps that speed from becoming chaos.
Introduce git status, diff views, commits, branches, stashes, editor undo, and session summaries.
Show how to look at what changed before giving another instruction.
Explain why known-good states matter before broad changes, migrations, or refactors.
Accept small verified changes, then continue with the next bounded step.

chapters.title: 6. Running Bash Commands
chapters.onScreenText: Read. Search. Test. Verify. Be careful with irreversible commands.
chapters.screenDirection: Terminal with commands and a side note listing command categories.
demoSteps: Ask the agent for the next smallest diagnostic command.
chapters.exercisePrompt: List five commands you are comfortable approving and five that require explicit review.
chapters.recap: Bash is where claims become checkable.
beats: Commands turn the agent's story into evidence.
Show read-only inspection, search, targeted tests, lint, typecheck, and local app startup.
Deletion, resets, network installs, migrations, production commands, credential access, and anything irreversible.
Ask the agent to run or suggest a search command and summarize what it proves.
Run a failing test or mocked failure. Ask the agent to reason from actual output.

chapters.title: 7. Permissions
chapters.onScreenText: What will it touch? Why now? What could go wrong?
chapters.screenDirection: Show a permission request example and annotate the decision.
demoSteps: Ask the agent to narrow it.
Record the policy in course notes.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write approval rules for network access, destructive commands, migrations, and broad file edits.
chapters.recap: Good permissions let the agent help while keeping irreversible decisions with you.
beats: Permission prompts are not friction. They are your chance to control blast radius.
File reads, file writes, shell commands, network access, browser access, credentials, and external services.
Compare reading a local file with deleting generated files, installing packages, running migrations, or calling production APIs.
What will it touch? Why is it needed? What could go wrong? Is there a narrower alternative?
Demonstrate denying "run setup" and approving "run the test command from package.json.

title: 03 - Day 1 Fundamentals: Detailed Video Scripts
subtitle: Script-driven draft video. Available from June 1, 2026.

chapters.title: 1. The Constraints Of LLMs
chapters.target: 12-15 minutes, concept lesson with side-by-side prompt comparison.
chapters.onScreenText: Fluent is not correct. Evidence beats confidence.
chapters.screenDirection: Ask a repo question without context, then ask again after inspecting files. Compare the answer quality.
demoSteps: Run or show one check that confirms a claim.
chapters.exercisePrompt: List three things an agent should verify before changing a real repo.
chapters.recap: LLMs are useful because they are fast and flexible. They become reliable when your process forces evidence.
beats: it can be fluent without being correct.
Explain that an LLM predicts likely text from context. That makes it useful for drafting, searching, and reasoning, but it does not make it a source of truth.
Name hallucinated functions, stale library knowledge, wrong file assumptions, broad refactors, and confident summaries that do not match the diff.
provide repo context, constrain scope, ask for file evidence, run commands, inspect diffs, and verify behavior.
Treat the agent like a fast collaborator inside a control loop. It helps you think and move faster; your workflow decides what is real.

chapters.title: 2. What Are Subagents
chapters.target: 10-13 minutes, workflow diagram plus delegation example.
chapters.screenDirection: Show one large task split into three lanes: code map, tests, docs. Merge findings into one main decision.
demoSteps: Identify one task not safe to delegate.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Take one large task and identify two safe subagent tasks plus one task you should keep yourself.
chapters.recap: Subagents reduce load when the work can be split cleanly. They do not remove responsibility.
beats: A subagent is not a replacement for your judgment. It is a bounded helper with a smaller job.
Explain parallel exploration, test inspection, doc review, research, or implementation in a clearly owned area.
A good subagent task is narrow, independent, observable, and has a clear output.
Look into this feature" creates overlap and contradictions. "Inspect tests for the billing path and return coverage gaps" is usable.
Product judgment, architecture tradeoffs, and cross-cutting decisions should stay in the main thread.

chapters.title: 3. Codebase Exploration
chapters.onScreenText: Explore before edit. File map before patch.
chapters.screenDirection: Terminal search on left, editor file map on right.
demoSteps: Open entry point, core logic, and tests.
Ask for a file map with evidence.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Pick one feature and create a three-file map: entry point, core logic, tests.
chapters.recap: Inspect the shape before you change the shape.
beats: Exploration is not delay. It is how the agent avoids touching the wrong part of the repo.
Identify files, entry points, call sites, tests, config, and docs.
Use fast search, file listing, route names, symbol names, test names, and imports.
Ask the agent to report which files matter, what each one does, and what evidence supports it.
Require the agent to label uncertainty. If it cannot prove a file matters, it should say so.

chapters.title: 4. Build A Feature
chapters.screenDirection: Add a small validation rule, CLI flag, UI field, or API response field.
demoSteps: Ask the agent to inspect existing pattern.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a feature brief with behavior, scope, likely files, and done condition.
chapters.recap: A feature is done when the behavior is verified and the diff is understandable.
beats: Feature work should be one thin slice, not a whole product area in one pass.
State what the user can do, what is in scope, what is not, and how success is checked.
Ask the agent to find how similar behavior is already implemented.
Change the smallest useful surface and avoid unrelated cleanup.
Run a targeted test, lint, typecheck, or manual flow.

chapters.title: 5. Non Determinism
chapters.onScreenText: Do not require identical output. Require bounded, verifiable output.
chapters.screenDirection: Run two prompt variants and show different outputs. Then tighten constraints and show convergence.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Rewrite a loose prompt so two runs would likely produce the same acceptable output.
chapters.recap: Non-determinism is managed with scope, constraints, and verification.
beats: If you ask the same model the same thing twice, you may not get the same answer. That is normal.
Explain generation choices, context changes, tool output differences, and different valid paths.
Planning, code style, file selection, naming, and explanations can vary.
Use tighter prompts, explicit constraints, examples, tests, repo instructions, and stable output formats.
Brainstorming and design alternatives benefit from multiple runs.

chapters.title: 6. Showing Context In The Status Line
chapters.screenDirection: Show two terminals: one ambiguous, one with visible repo/branch/task notes.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a before-edit status check with repo, branch, scope, and verification plan.
chapters.recap: Know where you are before you change anything.
beats: Long AI sessions get risky when nobody remembers the repo, branch, task, or mode.
Explain repo name, branch, dirty state, current task, permission mode, and environment.
Wrong repo, wrong branch, wrong command, uncommitted changes, or forgotten task scope.
Before major edits, confirm where you are, what you are changing, and how you will verify it.
Visible context makes compaction and handoff easier.

chapters.title: 7. Why Plan Mode Sucks
chapters.target: 10-13 minutes, compare generic plan to repo-grounded plan.
chapters.onScreenText: Do not plan in a vacuum.
chapters.screenDirection: Show a generic plan first, then inspect files and rewrite it with real file paths and checks.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Take a broad task and write a two-step discovery plan before implementation.
chapters.recap: Planning works when it stays tied to evidence and execution.
beats: Planning is useful. Planning in a vacuum creates fake certainty.
Plans written before repo evidence often invent architecture, miss constraints, and overgeneralize.
Generic steps, no file references, no commands, no verification, and no stop conditions.
Short plan, inspect, revise, execute one step, verify, then continue.
Ask for files, commands, risks, and acceptance criteria.

chapters.title: 8. The Grill Execute Clear Loop
chapters.screenDirection: Use one small bug or feature and run the whole loop.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Use the loop on a feature idea and write one sentence for each stage.
chapters.recap: The loop converts vague intent into repeatable progress.
beats: grill, execute, clear.
Ask hard questions about scope, acceptance, risks, tradeoffs, and unknowns.
Make one bounded slice with visible checks. No sprawling edits.
Summarize what changed, what was verified, what remains open, and what comes next.
It prevents drift and keeps humans, agents, and subagents aligned.

chapters.title: 9. Compaction
chapters.onScreenText: Goal. Decisions. Files. Checks. Risks. Next.
chapters.screenDirection: Turn a messy session transcript into a concise continuation note.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a compaction note for a completed lesson exercise.
chapters.recap: Compaction is state preservation, not just shortening.
beats: Long sessions eventually get too large. Compaction preserves what matters and drops noise.
Goal, constraints, decisions, files changed, checks run, unresolved risks, and next step.
A diary is not a continuation summary. A good compaction is a restart packet.
Before a new phase, after major decisions, before handoff, or when context gets messy.
Make it short, factual, and action-oriented.

chapters.title: 10. Handing Off
chapters.screenDirection: Draft a final handoff message after a small feature.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a handoff with four sections: done, verified, open, next.
chapters.recap: Good handoffs preserve momentum.
beats: A task is not handed off if the next person has to rediscover everything.
Goal, current state, changed files, decisions, checks, blockers, and next step.
Include exact file paths, exact commands, exact constraints, and known uncertainty.
Explain that complete for a slice is not the same as reviewed or merged.
If verification failed, say so directly and include output or next diagnostic step.

title: 04 - Day 2 Steering: Detailed Video Scripts
subtitle: Script-driven draft video. Available from June 1, 2026.

chapters.title: 1. What Is A Repo Instruction File
chapters.screenDirection: Create or inspect the repo instruction file your harness reads.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Draft five repo instructions you want an agent to know before editing.
chapters.recap: Repo instructions give the agent the local rules of the road.
beats: Every serious harness needs a way to learn the local rules of a repo.
Explain that this may be AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, opencode config, IDE custom instructions, or a linked project guide.
setup commands, tests, style, architecture notes, safety rules, and review expectations.
Huge docs, stale opinions, secrets, vague encouragement, and anything not actionable.
Project overview, commands, conventions, workflow rules, and escalation rules.

chapters.title: 2. Steering An Agent With Repo Instructions
chapters.screenDirection: Add a final-report rule, then ask the agent to do a tiny task and compare output.
demoSteps: Add to the harness-specific repo instruction file.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Identify one instruction you repeat often and rewrite it for your harness's repo instruction mechanism.
chapters.recap: Steering works when repo instructions are concrete enough to change behavior.
beats: If you repeat the same prompt every session, it probably belongs in durable repo instructions.
Code style, testing rules, branch rules, forbidden actions, preferred tools, and final report format.
Take a repeated instruction and make it durable.
Use rg for search" beats "search carefully." "Report files changed and checks run" beats "summarize well.
Run a tiny task and see if the agent follows the instruction.

chapters.title: 3. Progressive Disclosure
chapters.onScreenText: Enough context to act. More context when needed.
chapters.screenDirection: Start with a short prompt, then reveal a module note after the agent identifies the relevant area.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Split one long instruction document into top-level, module-level, and task-specific notes.
chapters.recap: Layered context keeps the agent oriented without drowning it.
beats: Dumping all context at once usually hides the part that matters.
Progressive disclosure means giving minimum useful context, then revealing more when the task needs it.
Top-level task, relevant docs, module rules, file-level conventions, and decision records.
Ambiguity, repeated mistake, new subsystem, failed verification, or risky decision.
Link deeper docs rather than forcing everything into one file.

chapters.title: 4. What Are Reusable Agent Workflows
chapters.screenDirection: Open a sample reusable workflow instruction and label each section.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Name one workflow you repeat often enough to save as a reusable instruction.
chapters.recap: Reusable workflows package repeatable expertise.
beats: A reusable workflow gives the agent a process to follow when a task needs more than a loose prompt.
Repeated work should not depend on copy-pasted prompts or memory.
TDD, diagnose, review, PRD, handoff, research, prototype.
Trigger, workflow, constraints, templates, examples, and references.
Prompts steer the current task; reusable workflows steer the process.

chapters.title: 5. Using Reusable Workflows For Steering
chapters.screenDirection: Invoke, attach, or paste a TDD or diagnose workflow on a small bug and point out each phase.
demoSteps: Invoke, attach, or paste the relevant workflow.
Review final output against workflow phases.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write a prompt that invokes or includes a reusable workflow and adds task-specific constraints.
chapters.recap: Use reusable workflows when you care about reliable process, not just an answer.
beats: Reusable workflows turn loose requests into structured processes.
Bug, feature, refactor, review, document, research, prototype, or handoff.
inspect, diagnose, test, implement, verify, summarize.
Reusable workflows reduce skipped reproduction, validation, and review.
A reusable workflow gives process; the prompt gives the local target and boundaries.

chapters.title: 6. Automatic Memory
chapters.target: 10-13 minutes, memory versus current evidence lesson.
chapters.screenDirection: Use a remembered preference, then verify a current command in the repo.
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write three things worth remembering and three things that must always be rechecked.
chapters.recap: Memory is helpful context, not a source of truth.
beats: Memory helps the agent start smarter, but it should not replace current evidence.
Preferences, recurring workflows, repo conventions, and prior decisions.
Current repo state, latest test result, dependency versions, active branch, or facts likely to change.
Memory can suggest; current files and commands confirm.
Ask the agent to use memory cautiously and refresh stale facts.

title: 05 - Day 3 Planning: Detailed Video Scripts
subtitle: Script-driven draft video. Available from June 1, 2026.

chapters.title: 1. How To Tackle Massive Tasks
chapters.screenDirection: Markdown plan with sections for unknowns, constraints, phases, validation.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Pick a large feature and write the goal, five unknowns, three constraints, and a three-phase plan.
chapters.recap: Big work becomes safe when you shrink uncertainty before asking for code.
beats: Massive tasks fail when the agent guesses too early.
Unclear requirements, many files, unknown architecture, multi-step integrations, or multi-day work.
Goal, constraints, unknowns, phases, tracer bullet, execution slices.
Ask the agent to inspect code, find integration points, and list open questions before editing.
Every phase needs a done condition, validation step, review gate, and stop condition.

chapters.title: 2. Write Great PRDs With A Reusable Workflow
chapters.screenDirection: Convert a vague feature request into PRD sections.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write three observable acceptance criteria for one feature.
chapters.recap: A good PRD reduces the number of decisions the agent has to guess.
beats: Agents cannot rescue unclear product thinking.
Problem, users, scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria, risks, rollout.
It interviews the user, exposes ambiguity, and forces tradeoffs before implementation.
Convert fuzzy wishes into observable behavior.
A PRD should sharpen work, not become a novel.

chapters.title: 3. Split Features Across Multiple Context Windows With Multi Phase Plans
chapters.screenDirection: Table with Phase, Goal, Inputs, Outputs, Checks, Handoff.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Create a three-phase plan where phase one proves the path end to end.
chapters.recap: Multi-phase plans let you use fresh context without losing the thread.
beats: One huge session loses detail and becomes hard to review.
Connected slices that can run in separate context windows.
Each phase needs goal, inputs, outputs, checks, and handoff.
Architecture or contract first, thin path next, expansion later.
Summarize decisions before switching windows.

chapters.title: 4. What Are Tracer Bullets
chapters.screenDirection: Draw request -> service -> database -> UI and highlight the thinnest path.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Identify the thinnest real end-to-end path for one feature.
chapters.recap: A tracer bullet proves the path before you invest in depth.
beats: A tracer bullet is the thinnest real end-to-end path through the system.
A prototype can be disposable; a tracer bullet touches the real layers.
It exposes integration points and reduces speculation.
One API field from request to DB to UI; one CLI flag from parser to output.
If it skips the risky integration, it did not prove the path.

chapters.title: 5. Use Tracer Bullets In Our Multi Phase Plan
chapters.screenDirection: Open phase table, rewrite first phase as tracer bullet, add review checklist.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Rewrite phase one of your plan so it proves one end-to-end path and defers the rest.
chapters.recap: The tracer bullet turns uncertainty into evidence.
beats: Phase one should answer the biggest integration question.
The easiest slice is not always the best first slice.
Define exactly what must be true for the tracer to count.
Polish, edge cases, performance, and full coverage come later.
Use tracer results to revise later phases.

chapters.title: 6. Executing Our Multi Phase Plan
chapters.screenDirection: Phase plan, agent prompt, diff, validation output, handoff note.
demoSteps: Connect it to the course workflow
chapters.exercisePrompt: Write the exact prompt you would use to execute phase one of your plan.
chapters.recap: Each phase must leave behind evidence.
beats: Do not execute a multi-phase plan as one giant prompt.
Give only the current phase plus necessary context, scope, and done condition.
Ask for a short implementation checklist after file inspection.
